title: 2–3. The soul is spiritual and separable from matter; VI hypotheses for teaching the highest good
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss: the highest good belonging toward man plus eternal beatitude cannot be taught fully enough plus distinctly — for until these stand as surveyed plus set beyond the cast belonging toward doubt. the state belonging toward its separation from the body, the resurrection belonging toward the flesh, plus what follows upon this — but here especially stands as to be considered the immortality belonging toward the rational soul. VI. But death stands as nothing other than the separation belonging toward the soul from the body. For experience teaches that same all die. It stands as separable from matter. 3. God stands as born, it says, with a human body plus likewise with the habit belonging toward having a rational plus incorporeal soul. or sixth ecumenical, sensed more holy in its eleventh action: — against all belonging toward whom the third Council belonging toward Constantinople. Against John, bishop belonging toward Thessalonica, who in the pseudo-synod belonging toward Nicaea, at the beginning belonging toward the fifth action, does not fear to say, toward establishing the cult belonging toward images, that same the Catholic Church believes every soul to be corporeal — with many philosophers belonging toward the Stoic plus Italic sects, with Tertullian plus a certain Apollinaris belonging toward Alexandria (of whom in the Tripartite History book 5, chapter 44), plus according to some with the Luciferians (Augustine, On heresies, chapter 81). and Hebrews 12:9. 2 Corinthians 7:1; 1 Corinthians 2:11 plus 1 Corinthians 6:20; Acts 7:60; Job 19:30; Luke 23:46; Matthew 27:50; Isaiah 26:9; second by all the places belonging toward Holy Scripture that same call the rational soul a spirit — as Ecclesiastes 12:7; that same which stand as far nobler than those that same can proceed from a corporeal thing; — this stands as shown first by its operations. It stands as belonging toward a spiritual nature. 2.
pass_b_english: 2. It is of a spiritual nature. This is shown first by its operations, which are far nobler than those that can proceed from a corporeal thing; second by all the places of Holy Scripture that call the rational soul a spirit — as [[Ecclesiastes 12:7>>Eccl. 12:7]]; [[Isaiah 26:9>>Esa. 26:9]]; [[Matthew 27:50>>Matth. 27:50]]; [[Luke 23:46>>Luc. 23:46]]; [[Job 19:30>>Job. 19:30]]; [[Acts 7:60>>Act. 7:60]]; [[1 Corinthians 2:11>>1 Cor. 2:11]] and [[1 Corinthians 6:20>>1 Cor. 6:20]]; [[2 Corinthians 7:1>>2 Cor. 7:1]]; and [[Hebrews 12:9>>Heb. 12:9]].

Against John, bishop of Thessalonica, who in the pseudo-synod of Nicaea, at the beginning of the fifth action, does not fear to say, for establishing the cult of images, that the Catholic Church believes every soul to be corporeal — with many philosophers of the Stoic and Italic sects, with Tertullian and a certain Apollinaris of Alexandria (of whom in the Tripartite History book 5, chapter 44), and according to some with the Luciferians (Augustine, On heresies, chapter 81).

Against all of whom the third Council of Constantinople, or sixth ecumenical, sensed more holy in its eleventh action: God is born, it says, with a human body and likewise with the habit of having a rational and incorporeal soul.
3. It is separable from matter. For experience teaches that all die. But death is nothing other than the separation of the soul from the body.

VI. But here especially is to be considered the immortality of the rational soul, the state of its separation from the body, the resurrection of the flesh, and what follows upon this. For until these are surveyed and set beyond the cast of doubt, the highest good of man and eternal beatitude cannot be taught fully enough and distinctly.
source_text: 2. Est naturae spiritualis. Hoc demonstrant, 1. illius operationes, quae multo nobiliores sunt, quam quae a re corporea proficisci possint. 2. Omnia S. Scripturae loca, quae animam rationalem spiritum appellant, ut Eccl. 12.7. Esa. 26.9. Matth. 27.50. Luc. 23.46. Job. 19.30. Act. 7.60. 1. Cor. 2.11. & 6.20. 2. Cor. 7.1. & Heb. 12.9. Contra Johannem Thessalonicensem episcopum, qui in pseudosynodo Nicena, initio actionis quintae, ad cultum imaginum adstruendum dicere non veretur, Catholicam ecclesiam credere omnem animam esse corpoream: cum multis Stoicae, Italicaeque sectae philosophis, cum Tertulliano & Apollinari quodam Alexandrino, de quo in hist. tripart. lib. 5. cap. 44. & juxta quosdam, Luciferianis, apud August. lib. haeres. cap. 81. Quibus omnibus sanctius sensit concilium tertium Constantinopolitanum, sive oecumenicum sextum, actione undecima: Nascitur, inquiens, Deus humano corpore similiterque & habitu animam rationalem & incorpoream habens. 3. Est separabilis a materia. Nam experientia docet omnes mori. Mors autem nihil aliud est, quam animae a corpore separatio. VI. Est autem hic potissimum consideranda animae rationalis immortalitas, status separationis illius a corpore, carnis resurrectio & quae hanc consequuntur. His enim nondum perspectis & extra dubii aleam positis, summum hominis bonum aeternaque beatitudo plene satis ac distincte doceri nequit.
